result: Progenitor cells contain on average ~26 centrioles, mature OSNs contain ~36 centrioles, and ~85% of centrioles in mature OSNs are associated with cilia (~31 cilia per knob). The majority of centrioles in mature OSNs originate from progenitor cells.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by expansion microscopy data with quantification (n=20 progenitor cells, n=24 mature OSNs from two mice). Sample sizes are modest but adequate for descriptive quantification. The inference that progenitors form the majority of centrioles (C35) is reasonable given the counts and is supported by prior work.

result: Centrioles migrate in multiple groups within a single OSN dendrite during dendrite outgrowth, with more groups found in the apical portion of the epithelium.
evaluation: Claims C6, C38, C27, C28 are supported by expansion microscopy imaging (Figure 2A) and are consistent with prior TEM observations (Heist and Mulvaney, 1968; Mulvaney and Heist, 1971). The observation of multiple groups per dendrite is clearly demonstrated.

result: Centriole migration occurs in tandem with dendrite extension. Centriole groups lag behind the dendrite tip by up to 8.4 µm, and microtubules are present both apical and basal to migrating centrioles.
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2B) showing centrioles in partially elongated dendrites with GAP43 and β-tubulin III staining. Sample size (n=12 dendrites, N=2 animals) is adequate for this descriptive observation.

result: Centrioles migrate slowly with a maximum rate of 0.18 µm/min. Most groups move apically, but ~1/3 show no net movement or basal movement during imaging. At this rate, centrioles could take >9.26 hr to traverse a 100 µm epithelium.
evaluation: Claims C7, C43-C45, C89 are supported by live imaging data (n=22 centriole groups, N=3 animals, Figure 2C-D). The calculation in C89 is straightforward arithmetic. The observation of bidirectional or stalled movement is interesting but the imaging window is limited, so net directionality over longer timescales is uncertain.

result: Migrating centrioles lack rootletin and are not held together by rootletin-based cohesion fibers. Some centrioles migrate singly. Rootletin is present in mature OSNs.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figure 3A). The absence of rootletin on migrating centrioles is clearly shown, and the antibody is validated by positive signal in mature OSNs and tissue culture cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The inference that cohesion fibers are absent (C47) is reasonable.

result: STIL and SASS6 are present on amplifying centrioles in progenitors and retained on some migrating centrioles in immature OSNs, but absent in mature OSNs. This suggests immature procentrioles can migrate, while mature OSNs contain mature centrioles lacking these markers.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 3B-C). The presence of STIL and SASS6 on migrating centrioles is clearly shown. The inferences (C53-C54) are reasonable given the data, though the exact proportion of migrating centrioles with these markers is not quantified.

result: Migrating OSN centrioles are associated with microtubule nucleation proteins (gamma-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, pericentrin) and PCM. In mature OSNs, gamma-tubulin and CDK5RAP2 remain, while pericentrin decreases.
evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 3D-F). The presence of PCM proteins on migrating centrioles is clearly demonstrated, distinguishing OSNs from many other neurons. The decrease in pericentrin in mature OSNs is noted but not quantified.

result: In immature OSNs near the apical surface with multiple centrioles, a single cilium is present. This cilium is associated with the centriole bearing distal appendages (CEP164), confirming centriole asymmetry. The parental centriole forms a cilium before other centrioles.
evaluation: Claims C62-C64, C12, C71 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4A, A'). The observation of a single cilium with CEP164 on one centriole is clear. The inference that this is the parental centriole (C71) is reasonable given the context of other data (C11, C68).

result: In mature OSNs with multiple cilia, many centrioles acquire distal appendages, indicating centriole maturation and remodeling occur at the apical surface.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C10 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figure 4B). The acquisition of CEP164 by multiple centrioles in mature OSNs is clearly shown. The inference that maturation occurs at the apical surface (C66) is reasonable.

result: During migration and amplification, only a single centriole (the parental centriole) has distal and subdistal appendages. Centriole modifications required for ciliogenesis occur after migration.
evaluation: Claims C11, C68-C70 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4C, 4—figure supplement 1A-C). The presence of appendages on a single centriole is clearly shown. The hypothesis (C67) is reasonable and supported by prior work. The inference (C70) is well-supported.

result: The parental centriole retains a unique centriolin configuration (radial subdistal appendage pattern) in mature OSNs, while other centrioles have single centriolin foci (basal feet). This unique structural characteristic distinguishes the parental centriole's cilium.
evaluation: Claims C13, C73-C76 are supported by expansion microscopy data (Figures 4D-E, 4—figure supplement 1B, D). The unique centriolin pattern on one centriole is clearly shown. The inference (C76) is reasonable and consistent with findings in MMCCs (C72).

result: A novel air-liquid interface explant culture system was developed. Explants remain viable, synthesize DNA, amplify centrioles, and retain tissue architecture. Paclitaxel treatment (microtubule stabilization) causes accumulation of centriole groups, particularly in the subapical compartment, suggesting microtubule dynamics are required for centriole migration to the apical surface.
evaluation: Claims C14, C77-C88 are supported by explant culture data (Figures 5B-F). EdU incorporation demonstrates viability. Paclitaxel treatment shows a 2.58-fold increase in subapical centriole groups at 6 hr (p=0.0084 by paired permutation test, N=2 animals). The statistical test is appropriate for paired data. Sample size is limited (N=2) but the effect is consistent and statistically significant. The inference (C88) is reasonable.

result: A model is proposed for centriole amplification in OSNs: rosette formation around parental centrioles in progenitors, followed by mitotic division, centriole disengagement, and further amplification in post-mitotic OSNs. This results in centrioles of three different ages in immature OSNs.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 represent a model/inference based on the current data and prior work (Ching and Stearns, 2020). The model is parsimonious and consistent with the centriole counts (C33-C35) and the presence of markers of different maturation states (C50-C54). However, it remains a model requiring further validation.

result: A portion of amplified centrioles in immature OSNs have undergone centriole-to-centrosome conversion, as evidenced by PCM proteins.
evaluation: Claim C94 is an inference supported by the presence of PCM proteins (C55-C61) and citations to prior work on centriole-to-centrosome conversion. The inference is reasonable but the exact proportion is not quantified.

result: Final modification of non-parental centrioles with rootlets, distal appendages, and subdistal appendages appears to be controlled spatially/temporally by arrival at the dendritic knob.
evaluation: Claim C95 is an inference supported by the observation that these components are absent on migrating centrioles (C46, C10) but present in mature OSNs (C49, C65). The inference is reasonable but the mechanism is not directly tested.

result: The presence of a single cilium before formation of multiple cilia might enable signaling important for OSN differentiation.
evaluation: Claim C96 is speculation (evidence_type: SPECULATION) based on analogy to MMCCs. The authors note that the earliest OSN cilia lack olfactory receptors (C97), which weakens the signaling hypothesis. No direct evidence is provided.

result: OSNs detect odorants using multiple cilia that protrude from the dendrite and require centrioles for formation. Cilia provide specialized membrane for olfactory receptor signaling, and disruption causes anosmia.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C17 are established knowledge supported by citations. These are foundational facts about OSN biology and cilium structure.

result: Centrioles in OSNs originate in progenitor cells near the basal lamina (50-100 µm from apical surface). Centriole amplification occurs in mitotically active progenitors before mitotic divisions are completed, which is unique among multiciliated cells. OSN differentiation and maturation follow a well-characterized timeline.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C18-C25 are supported by citations to prior work, including the authors' previous study (Ching and Stearns, 2020) and other established literature. These provide essential context for the current study.

result: Prior work has observed migrating centrioles in OSNs by TEM and in C. elegans PQR neurons. Vertebrate OSNs contain multiple centrioles that migrate over greater distances (10-fold) than C. elegans and develop throughout life.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are supported by citations to prior work. These provide context for the novelty of the current study. The 10-fold distance comparison (C31) is a reasonable inference from the stated distances (5 µm vs 50-100 µm).

result: Prior work in MMCCs and C. elegans neurons provides relevant comparisons for centriole migration mechanisms, including parental centriole identity, effects of microtubule stabilization, dynein involvement, and microtubule polarity in dendrites.
evaluation: Claims C72, C98-C104 are supported by citations to prior work. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings and proposing mechanisms.

result: Migrating centrioles are associated with microtubule nucleation factors but acquire rootletin and appendages only in mature OSNs.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 summarize findings detailed in other claim groups (C55-C61 for nucleation factors, C46-C49 for rootletin, C10, C65 for appendages). These are well-supported by the data.

result: Dividing progenitors require multiple days to give rise to fully mature OSNs.
evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by citations to prior work (Rodriguez-Gil et al., 2015; McClintock et al., 2020). This provides context for the calculated migration time (C89).
